extracted.intended_audience: USCIS adjudicators, DHS policymakers, immigration attorneys, advocates, and stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural guidance for determining whether a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge, including what factors to consider, evidentiary expectations, exemptions, and officer duties. Applies to USCIS/DHS officers implementing the final rule and to stakeholders interpreting its operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Each public charge inadmissibility determination must be individualized and based on the evidence presented in the specific case; adjudicators must consider the totality of the individual's circumstances rather than assigning predetermined weight to particular factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS retains the longstanding 'totality of the circumstances' approach (as in the 1999 Interim Field Guidance) and declines to codify a system of weighted negative/positive factors. Officers may consider all information or evidence in the record relevant to a public charge inadmissibility determination. DHS may periodically issue guidance and empirical analyses to inform how factors may affect likelihood of becoming a public charge, and will train officers accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 212(a)(4) calls for consideration, at minimum, of age, health, family status, assets/resources and financial status, and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five factors form the baseline of the totality analysis; DHS has clarified what information is relevant to many of these factors in the rule and Form I-485. No one of these factors (other than lack of a sufficient Affidavit of Support when required) should be the sole criterion for determining public charge inadmissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age (statutory factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Age is a statutory factor to be considered in the totality of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will consider age alongside other statutory factors; commenters urged that age should not be given determinative weight because it can disproportionately affect certain groups. DHS maintains that age should be one factor among many in a case-by-case analysis and not assigned preset 'heavy' weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health (statutory factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Health is a statutory factor, including consideration of disabilities and any current or past institutionalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS clarifies that the presence of a disability, as defined by section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, is not alone a sufficient basis to determine a person is likely to become a public charge. Officers assessing past or current institutionalization should take into account evidence that such institutionalization was in violation of Federal law (e.g., ADA or Section 504), and unjustified confinement should not contribute to a public charge finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family status (statutory factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Family status is one of the five statutory factors to be considered in the totality of the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family circumstances (e.g., dependents) are to be weighed with other factors and are not to be treated as inherently determinative; evidence relevant to family status should be collected as outlined in the rule and forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assets, resources, and financial status (statutory factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assets, resources, and financial status are statutory factors to be considered when assessing likelihood of becoming a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will consider assets/resources/financial status in context with other factors. DHS rejects categorical presumptions about assets (and declines to adopt presumptions) because such presumptions often can be overcome by other favorable factors in an individual's circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and skills (statutory factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Education and skills are statutory factors relevant to the totality analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will consider an applicant's education and skills as part of the overall assessment. DHS declines to give preset greater weight to education and income absent comparative empirical evidence showing they are more predictive than other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA
rubrics_metrics.description: A sufficient Affidavit of Support, where required, should be favorably considered in the totality of the circumstances and the lack of a sufficient Affidavit of Support is the only factor that may be treated as controlling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will 'favorably consider' a sufficient 213A affidavit; the rule states that no one factor 'other than the lack of a sufficient Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA, if required, should be the sole criterion' for public charge determinations. DHS may consider an affidavit as part of assets/resources/financial status factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of home- and community-based services (HCBS)
rubrics_metrics.description: HCBS are excluded from consideration in public charge inadmissibility determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After consultation with HHS, DHS determined to exclude HCBS because they 'help older adults and persons with disabilities live, work, and fully participate in their communities' and do not provide 'total care for basic needs' (they do not pay for room and board).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of institutionalization and evidence of unlawful confinement
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing past or current institutionalization, officers will take into account, when applicable, any evidence that institutionalization violated Federal law (e.g., ADA or Rehabilitation Act), and unjustified confinement should not contribute to a public charge finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule recognizes that some institutionalization may have occurred in violation of anti-discrimination laws; adjudicators should consider relevant evidence submitted by noncitizens to support such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-determinative treatment of disability or age alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a disability or being a child (or other single characteristic) alone is not sufficient to determine that a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states that disability (as defined by section 504) will not alone be a sufficient basis to determine public charge risk. DHS also rejects the 2019 Final Rule's additional negative weighting for children under 18 and for disability/health, finding such weights discriminatory and unduly prescriptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written explanation requirement for denials
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS officers must explain in writing the specific reasons for a denial, and written denial decisions based on public charge must 'reflect consideration of each of the factors ... and specifically articulate the reasons for the officer's determination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS is codifying the requirement that written denials include a discussion of each factor to ensure decisions are case-by-case and based on statutory factors and guidance; this acts as a safeguard against subjective or biased decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions and treatment of benefits received while in exempt status
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits received while a noncitizen was present in an immigration category exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility (as listed in 8 CFR 212.23(a)) or received a waiver (8 CFR 212.23(c)) will not be considered in public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, benefits received prior to or subsequent to exempt status may be considered, and applicants may submit mitigating information for DHS to consider. DHS will explicitly list statutory and regulatory exemptions in the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of mitigating circumstances for temporary benefit use
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers should consider the circumstances underlying a person's use of benefits (e.g., domestic violence, crime, public health or natural disaster, economic downturn, pregnancy, having a new child) as temporary use may help individuals regain stability and not predict future need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters urged guidance to limit consideration of factors that would unfairly penalize survivors; DHS notes many survivors are exempt, but allows mitigating information to be included in the totality assessment and will permit consideration of such context where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disallowing attribution of other household members' benefit use to applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefit use by other household members (including U.S. citizen children) should not be attributed to the noncitizen applicant for public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS rejects 'household' attribution approaches used in some analyses and states the household is not the proper unit of analysis for public charge determinations; only benefits received by the noncitizen and where the noncitizen is listed as a beneficiary are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: No presumptions or codified weightings
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS will not create legal presumptions (e.g., presuming persons with certain assets/resources or certain categories are or are not public charges) nor codify weighted factors; instead DHS uses the totality approach without assigning fixed weights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS explains that presumptions would often be overcome by other factors and that weighting would provide a misleading mathematical precision; DHS will, however, 'favorably consider' a sufficient Affidavit of Support and may issue guidance to generally inform the predictive nature of factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of evidence and initial supporting evidence requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS is collecting initial information related to the enumerated factors on Form I-485 and generally is not requiring submission of initial supporting evidence except where required (e.g., evidence that institutionalization violated Federal law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While initial supporting evidence is limited, DHS may consider any relevant evidence in the record (e.g., certification/approval to receive cash assistance, letters from sponsoring institutions) and applicants may submit mitigating information for consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of letters from sponsoring institutions and other record evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS has discretion to consider relevant information in the record, including letters from sponsoring institutions (e.g., indicating income/insurance commitments) that bear on assets/resources/financial status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when a 213A affidavit is not required, information such as a sponsor letter may be relevant to the assets/resources factor and overall totality assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical data, guidance, training, and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS intends to periodically issue guidance informed by empirical analyses of best-available data, to train officers, and to maintain oversight and quality control to promote fair and consistent determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will update guidance as appropriate; USCIS plans robust officer training. DHS acknowledges current data collection limits in adjudicative IT systems but intends to collect relevant information via form changes (Form I-485) and other means to support empirical assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that decisions adapt to unique fact patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Because each noncitizen's circumstances form a unique fact pattern, outcomes in public charge determinations will appropriately vary and adjudicators must adapt analysis to specific case facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS emphasizes individualized determinations, reiterates that officers must consider all statutory factors and evidence in the record, and rejects categorical or mechanistic rules that would preclude case-by-case assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited initial automated data capture and manual review needs
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS adjudicative systems do not currently allow comprehensive automated data collection of public charge denials; some manual review of administrative files is required to analyze denials under 212(a)(4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes limitations of older systems (CLAIMS3) versus newer systems (ELIS) and indicates ongoing efforts to collect better data for adjudication analysis and training, but recognizes current technical limitations.
